bounds: One CLI controller, one synchronous worker, one checker process, two sequential cases, one graceful or forced cancellation. SIGINT and SIGTERM share the cancellation transition.
fairness: CleanupProgress assumes fair signal forwarding, expiry of the finite grace timer, kernel delivery of forced termination and process reaping. Uncatchable termination of the supervisor is outside the model.
limitations: The model projects a process group to one checker. Independently daemonized process groups are outside this ownership boundary.

The implementation conformance runs all 28 runner checks on Linux, including real Node parent/child/grandchild cancellation, inventory receipt retention, source-change rejection and scenario selection through parameterized imports. Other platforms run 26 checks and explicitly skip the two Linux process-group schedules. Compiler semantic correctness remains in each source model.
Operating-system process and Job Object semantics are platform assumptions. Linux conformance is exercised in this repository's Quint CI job.

Nested cancellation models one managed worker group, a pending child spawn, and a worker exiting before its checker. The Linux real-process tests delay the owned controller group by 500 ms and exercise SIGINT/SIGTERM for both existing and late checker descendants.

assumptions: Checked formula in RunnerCancellation: CleanupProgress = (forward.weakFair(s) and force.weakFair(s) and reap.weakFair(s)).implies( s.cancelled.leadsTo(s.phase == "done"))
The property is conditional on its written model fairness and environmental premises. Real scheduler fairness, provider completion and implementation refinement are not proved.

Weak fairness of cleanup-clock ticks and reaping. The direct controller dispatches its three-second cleanup before the enclosing ten-second grace. Arbitrary external suspension of the controller beyond that allowance and uncatchable controller termination are excluded.
